title: Change Order Form | Free Word Template
description: Free change order form: document scope, cost or timeline changes on a project with signed approval.
lead: A written form used on construction, freelance and other project work to document a change to scope, price or timeline — signed by both client and contractor before the extra work proceeds.
introParagraphs: A change order form (or variation order) documents an agreed change to a project — extra work, changed specifications, schedule adjustments, or price changes. Signed by both parties, it amends the original contract and keeps scope creep from turning into payment disputes.
Always get change orders signed before doing the extra work. Verbal change orders are a top cause of contractor-client disputes.
bullets: Project and parties
Client and contractor names; project name/address; original contract date; change order number.
Description of change
Specific description of the changed work, which original contract clause/drawing/SOW it amends, and why the change is needed.
Cost impact
Added/deducted cost broken down (labour, materials, subcontractor, overhead/markup); net change in contract price; revised total contract value.
Schedule impact
Number of days added/deducted; revised substantial completion date; any delay costs.
Signatures
Authorised signatories for both client and contractor; date of signature; statement that this change order amends the contract.
howTo: Describe the change precisely
Reference the original drawings/spec and explain exactly what is changing — vague change orders create later disputes.
Price the work
Break down labour, materials, markup and taxes; show the new total contract price.
Calculate schedule impact
State how many days the job is extended (or shortened) and the new completion date.
Sign before work starts
Do not start changed work without a signed change order; if urgent, confirm by email and follow with signature.
Attach supporting docs
Attach new drawings, specs, quotes or photos as exhibits to the change order.
related: Original scope document this change order amends.
Master agreement that usually requires change orders for scope changes.
Used when a project is terminated instead of changed.
faq: Is a change order binding?
Once signed by both authorised parties, yes — it amends the original contract.
Can the contractor do extra work without one?
Technically yes, but they may not get paid if the client disputes the scope was agreed; always get one signed.
Who signs?
Representatives with authority to change the contract — typically the project owner and a principal/PM of the contractor.
What if I need a change urgently?
Proceed on a written email approval documenting cost and schedule impact, then convert to a signed change order within days.
Do change orders affect warranty?
Changed work is typically warranted the same way as the original unless the CO specifies otherwise.

title: Catering Contract | Free Word Template
description: Free catering contract: set menu, pricing, service, headcount, deposits and cancellation terms for events.
lead: A contract between a caterer and a client for food and beverage service at an event — covering menu, guest count, staffing, rentals, timeline, deposits and cancellation.
introParagraphs: A catering contract sets out the food, drink, service and pricing for an event (wedding, corporate event, party). It locks in the menu, headcount, service style, rentals, staff, timeline and payment schedule.
Catering has many moving parts and perishable costs. Specify final headcount deadlines, cancellation/refund terms, dietary accommodations, and who supplies tables/linen/bar to avoid day-of surprises.
bullets: Client and caterer
Caterer business, contact and license info; client name, phone and email; event date, time and venue.
Menu and service

Detailed menu (starters, mains, sides, desserts, drinks), service style (buffet, plated, family style, stations), dietary accommodations (vegetarian, vegan, allergies), and bar service (host vs cash).
Pricing and headcount
Per-person price or fixed price, minimum guest count, final headcount deadline (typically 7-14 days before), service charge/gratuity and taxes.
Staff and rentals
Number of servers, bartenders, chefs; rentals provided (tables, chairs, linens, china, glassware vs client-provided); setup and cleanup times.
Deposits, cancellation and liability
Deposit amount and due date, final payment deadline, cancellation/refund schedule (closer to event = less refundable), food safety, alcohol compliance/licensing, insurance and indemnity.
howTo: Confirm menu and tasting
Offer a tasting before signing for larger events; finalise menu and dietary options.
Lock the date with a deposit
Collect a non-refundable deposit (25-50%) to reserve the date; specify refund schedule for cancellations.
Set headcount deadline
Require a final guest count 7-14 days before the event; price will be based on that number.
Clarify rentals and staffing
Spell out who provides what (linen, tables, bar, staffing); include setup/teardown windows.
Get permits and insurance
Confirm venue insurance requirements, health permits and liquor licensing; name the venue as additional insured if required.
related: Used alongside for full-service event planning.
If the caterer wants to photograph food for portfolio.
Often required by venues for caterers.
For alcohol service and potential injury claims.
faq: How much deposit is typical?
25-50% of the estimated total; non-refundable within a set window before the event.
Who pays for no-shows?
The client pays for the guaranteed final headcount even if some guests do not show up.
Do I need a liquor license?
If serving alcohol, yes — either the caterer must be licensed or the venue must cover it; cash bars have additional requirements.
What about dietary restrictions?
Ask guests for dietary needs in advance and include a clause that the caterer will provide labelled options.
What if the venue has an exclusive caterer?
Many venues do — confirm the client is allowed to bring in an outside caterer before signing.

title: Event Planning Contract | Free Word Template
description: Free event planning contract: set scope, fees, vendor management, deposits and cancellation for event planners.
lead: A contract between an event planner and a client defining the planning services, scope, fees, vendor coordination, payment schedule and cancellation terms for an event.
introParagraphs: An event planning contract covers the services an event planner will provide for a wedding, corporate event, party or conference — venue scouting, vendor management, timeline, day-of coordination, budget management and communication.
Be precise about scope: 'full planning' vs 'day-of coordination' are very different engagements. Set limits on hours, revisions and meetings to avoid scope creep.
bullets: Client and planner
Event planner name/business; client name(s); event date(s) and venue (if known); date of agreement.
Scope of services
Specific services included (venue search, vendor coordination, budget management, design, day-of coordination, RSVP tracking) and what is excluded (catering, venue fees, decor costs).
Fees and payment
Flat fee, percentage of budget, or hourly rate; deposit/retainer amount; payment milestones; reimbursement policy for expenses; any referral commissions disclosed.
Client responsibilities
Timely decisions, budget approvals, vendor payments outside planner scope, guest list management, and accessibility requirements.
Cancellation, liability and IP
Cancellation/postponement terms and refund schedule; force majeure; liability limits; insurance; photo rights for portfolio; and governing law.
howTo: Define the package clearly
List exactly what is included — full planning, partial, month-of, or day-of coordination.
Disclose fees and commissions
State how you are paid (flat fee, percentage, referral commissions); transparency builds trust and complies with industry standards.
Set a revision/meeting limit
Include a number of included meetings/revisions to avoid endless scope.
Specify payment milestones
Deposit on signing, progress payments leading up to the event, final balance due before the event day.
Include force majeure
Pandemics, weather, venue closures — state what happens to deposits/fees if the event is postponed or canceled by forces outside either party control.",
related: Caterer-specific contract; often coordinated under the planner.
faq: What percentage do planners typically charge?
10-20% of total event budget for full planning; flat fees or day-of rates are also common.
Do I need a separate contract for day-of coordination?
Yes — day-of coordination is a different scope; use a shorter agreement listing the specific coordination duties.
What about vendor deposits?
Clarify whether clients pay vendors directly or through the planner; you are not a bank unless explicitly stated.
Who is liable for vendor no-shows?
Planner should act in good faith but not guarantee third parties; liability limits and force majeure help.
What if the client cancels?
Non-refundable deposit; sliding-scale refund based on how far out cancellation happens.

title: Photo Release Form | Free Word Template
description: Free photo release form: get permission to use a person likeness or photos in marketing, portfolio or publications.
lead: A signed form granting permission to use an individual photograph, video or likeness in marketing materials, portfolio, publications, social media or other uses — specifying what uses are allowed and whether compensation is paid.
introParagraphs: A photo release (or model release) is signed by a person (or parent/guardian of a minor) giving you permission to use photographs or footage that show their face, likeness or identifiable features. You need one for commercial/portfolio use — publishing someone image without permission can violate right-of-publicity laws.
Editorial use (news, commentary) generally does not require a release, but marketing, advertising, stock photography, branded social media and commercial portfolios always do.
bullets: Photographer and subject
Photographer/company name; subject name and contact (parent/guardian if minor); date of shoot.
Description of media
Which photos/videos/footage the release covers (event, shoot date, or general ongoing permission).
Grant of rights
What uses are permitted (marketing, portfolio, social media, advertising, editorial, worldwide, perpetual) and what is excluded.
Compensation
Whether consideration is provided (payment, prints, CD/TFP, or just voluntary); confirm release is binding without separate payment if free.
Waiver and signature
Waiver of right to inspect/approve finished product, release of claims, subject signature (and parent/guardian for minors), date.
howTo: Use the right release
Use a model release for identifiable people; a property release for private property; a minor release signed by a parent/guardian for children.
Specify usage broadly
State 'marketing, advertising, portfolio, social media, website' etc. to avoid needing a new form for each platform.
Get it signed before shooting
Have subjects sign before photography begins; it is harder to get after you have taken pictures.
Keep copies filed
Store releases with the photos they cover — you may need to show them years later.
For minors, parent signature required
A minor cannot sign their own release; a parent or legal guardian must sign.
related: Often bundled with releases for events.
For settling claims; different from image use.
Service contract between photographer and client; release often included.
Video equivalent; talent releases for footage.
faq: Do I need a release for candid event photos?
For private events, yes; for public-street editorial use, generally not for adults, but best practice is a release for commercial/marketing use.
Do employees need to sign?
Yes, if you will use their photo in company marketing — include in onboarding paperwork or get a separate release.
Does a social-media tag count as permission?
No — get a written release; implicit consent is risky.
Is a release needed for group event photos?
For public events a posted notice plus ticket language can substitute; for small groups get individual releases.
How long does it last?
Most releases are perpetual and worldwide; if you want to limit, specify the term.

title: Remote Work Agreement | Free Word Template
description: Free remote work agreement: set expectations for employees working from home — hours, equipment, security and expenses.
lead: An agreement between employer and employee setting expectations for remote/hybrid work: work location, hours, availability, equipment provision, data security, expense reimbursement and time tracking.
introParagraphs: A remote work agreement (or telecommuting agreement) sets out the ground rules for employees working from home or another remote location. It covers work hours, availability response times, equipment provided by the company, data security, expense reimbursement, health and safety.
A good remote work agreement protects company data (a major remote-work risk), clarifies expectations, and ensures both sides understand how performance will be measured.
bullets: Employee and role
Employee name, role/title, manager; effective date; whether fully remote or hybrid (and expected in-office days).
Work location and hours
Approved remote work address; core working hours; expected response time for messages; time zone; overtime approval process.
Equipment and expenses
Company-provided equipment (laptop, monitor, phone), office stipend if any, internet/phone reimbursement, and who covers repairs/replacement.
Security and confidentiality
Secure internet connection, VPN, device encryption, handling confidential information, no-use-of-personal-devices rules, data breach reporting and return of equipment on termination.
Performance, leave and termination
How performance is measured (output-based), time-off requests, workers comp for home injuries, right to end the remote arrangement, and return of equipment on termination.
howTo: Set clear availability expectations
Define core hours and response times so collaboration works across time zones.
Provide security training
Pair the agreement with security training (VPN, phishing, physical device security).
Clarify equipment ownership
State what equipment is company property and must be returned; who is responsible for damage/loss.
Address expense reimbursement
Some states require employers to reimburse necessary work-from-home expenses; be explicit about internet, phone and office stipends.
Make it revocable
Reserve the company right to end remote work or require return to office with reasonable notice; review the agreement periodically.
related: Base employment contract this agreement supplements.
Confidentiality obligations amplified for remote work.
Defines the role expectations measured in remote work.
faq: Is remote work a permanent change?
It can be, but make it revocable with notice — business needs change.
Do I have to reimburse internet/phone?
Several US states (CA, IL, MA, MT, IA, DC, NH, PA, others) require reimbursement of necessary business expenses incurred by employees working from home.
Who is liable for injuries at home?
Workers compensation generally covers work-related injuries even when working from home; encourage a safe workspace.
Can I require in-office days?
Yes in most places — specify in-office days in the agreement or handbook.
Do I need to track hours?
For non-exempt employees you must track hours (including overtime) regardless of location; consider time-tracking tools.
